extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, FERC, state public utility commissions, utilities and electricity-sector stakeholders (e.g., cooperatives)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal legal and technical comments on EPA's proposed Clean Power Plan (CAA §111(d)), addressing jurisdictional limits, market and tariff constraints, reliability, and fuel/infrastructure implications of any required 'beyond-the-fence' measures such as environmental dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Power Act scope / federal jurisdiction over wholesale sales and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Power Act vests the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) with exclusive jurisdiction to regulate wholesale sales of electricity and the transmission of electricity in interstate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 16 U.S.C. § 824; explains that wholesale sales and interstate transmission fall squarely within FERC's authority and that federal regulation of those matters was intended as a national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulation limited to distribution, retail service, and certain siting/constructive approvals (CPCN)
rubrics_metrics.description: States regulate electric distribution (to the extent facilities are not used for interstate transmission), regulate rates/terms/conditions of retail electric service, and may require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) for building new plants or transmission in the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A CPCN requires a state determination that construction is consistent with the public interest; once granted the State's role is generally limited to environmental oversight and cost recovery through retail rate regulation. The authority to grant a CPCN does not necessarily give a State the authority to revoke it because the plant uses a disfavored fuel or to require the generator to operate less than provided in the certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: State authority over IRPs is limited and subject to state-law balancing of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In traditionally regulated States, PUCs generally review and guide utilities' integrated resource plans (IRPs), which are plans for meeting demand via supply- and demand-side resources over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRPs help guide long-term utility decisions but state law governs the criteria PUCs must use; environmental concerns are only one criterion and PUCs must balance all statutorily defined state interests. Under the regulatory compact, PUCs cannot deny cost recovery for prudent investments already made and used-and-useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits in restructured states and over independent power producers (IPPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In restructured States, PUCs have ceded resource choices to competitive energy suppliers and cannot direct those suppliers to use more or less of any fuel. PUCs likewise lack authority over resource decisions by independent power producers (wholesale generators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive wholesale generators sell at rates, terms, and conditions regulated by FERC and make resource investment decisions based on market value; state PUCs cannot compel dispatch or resource mixes for these entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) and energy efficiency mandates are state-law creations and vary widely
rubrics_metrics.description: Most RPSs and energy efficiency mandates are enacted by state legislatures (not unilaterally by PUCs) and differ dramatically across States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The levels, eligible resource types, compliance deadlines, and methods of implementation reflect diverse state judgments about costs, benefits, and consumer willingness to spend for those policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: PUC prudence review is focused on cost and financial risk, not emissions minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing jurisdictional utility costs, PUCs review the prudence of a utility's decisions with the primary focus on minimizing cost and financial risk to retail consumers, not on minimizing emissions of a single pollutant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, PUCs generally cannot direct utilities to change past investment decisions or operations solely to achieve emissions reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filed Rate Doctrine / operators bound to FERC-approved tariffs
rubrics_metrics.description: All jurisdictional wholesale sales and transmission services must be provided pursuant to FERC-approved tariffs; under the Filed Rate Doctrine operators are bound to the rates, terms, and conditions that FERC has approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only rates fixed or accepted by FERC may be charged; not even state or federal courts can authorize a utility to charge a different rate. This constrains state or EPA attempts to force departures from filed tariffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISO/RTO market rules and security-constrained economic dispatch are FERC-filed and binding
rubrics_metrics.description: ISOs and RTOs operate organized markets that evaluate demand and available supply and apply rules (e.g., security constrained economic dispatch) to select least-cost generation to meet demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tariffs and market rules are filed with and approved by FERC; the important point for the Proposed Rule is that these terms are FERC-approved and neither EPA nor the States can unilaterally alter them.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC is not an environmental regulator and historically has not ordered environmental dispatch preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC has facilitated variable renewable participation in wholesale markets but has never required a generation dispatch preference based on emissions characteristics or otherwise set an environmental dispatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's assumption that dispatch order can be restructured for emissions reasons does not reflect FERC's historical role or actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy Clause bars state actions that intrude on FERC's exclusive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has held that States may not regulate in areas where FERC has properly exercised jurisdiction to determine just and reasonable wholesale rates or to insure that agreements affecting wholesale rates are reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any state action that directly or indirectly modifies how electricity is sold at wholesale or transmitted in interstate commerce could impermissibly intrude on FERC's exclusive jurisdiction and be inconsistent with the Supremacy Clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot force charges or rates not on file with FERC (case law: Mississippi Power & Nantahala)
rubrics_metrics.description: States may not order utilities to charge rates or allocate capacity in ways that conflict with FERC-approved contracts or tariffs; courts have overturned state decisions that conflict with FERC-approved terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mississippi Power & Light Co. v. Mississippi and Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. Thornburg illustrate that FERC's exclusive jurisdiction applies not only to rates but to capacity allocations affecting wholesale rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: State actions that undermine FERC tariffs or market structures risk preemption even if for legitimate state objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws that change procurement or contracting to favor certain resources can be struck down when they affect prices or allocations in FERC-regulated markets (e.g., ISO-NE and PPL EnergyPlus cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tariffs approved by FERC affecting state RPS implementation; Fourth Circuit striking down Maryland law directing contracts with a select generator because it 'affected' capacity prices in a FERC market.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's 'beyond-the-fence' BSER assumptions may improperly presume state authority over FERC-jurisdictional matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule's assertion that states will redirect dispatch to substitute high-emitting generators with lower-emitting ones assumes states can regulate activities that are subject to FERC jurisdiction or otherwise beyond their authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because much dispatch occurs in wholesale markets under FERC jurisdiction, EPA's reliance on states to effect environmental dispatch is constitutionally and practically problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional power markets may not be prepared to implement an environmental dispatch obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation assumes infrastructure, market incentives, and regional consensus that may not exist; redesigning markets to accomplish environmental dispatch involves substantial uncertainty and time and could compromise reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative scenario: a State seeking to change dispatch in a multi-state ISO (e.g., MISO) would need near-consensus among many states and market participants, and any tariff changes would face negotiation, FERC approval, and likely litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market redesign for environmental dispatch is slow, contested, and requires broad stakeholder agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: To change tariff rules or ISO/RTO market design to achieve environmental dispatch, stakeholders must negotiate, the ISO/RTO board must approve, FERC must approve the tariff, and courts may be asked to review the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different stakeholders (owners of low- and high-emitting resources, consumer advocates, states focused on affordability) have divergent interests; changes could create congestion and higher prices for some consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC must confront whether approving an environmental re-dispatch tariff is 'just and reasonable'
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC would have to decide if its responsibility to ensure just and reasonable rates permits approving a tariff that increases rates above economic dispatch or discriminates against certain resources based on CO2 emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any FERC decision on such a novel question would likely be followed by appeals to the courts of appeals, creating protracted uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability obligations under Section 215 / NERC standards must be preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 215 authorizes FERC to oversee the reliable operation of the Nation’s interconnected bulk power system; FERC-approved mandatory national reliability standards (administered by NERC) require entities to respond to emergencies, maintain reserves, protect equipment, and follow load-shedding instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental regulation must be designed and coordinated so as not to impair grid reliability; any re-dispatch regime must account for NERC and FERC reliability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must coordinate with FERC (and rely on FERC/NERC expertise) when evaluating reliability impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's Proposed Rule must address how environmental dispatch will be required or enforced in light of FERC's primary and exclusive role over reliability standards; EPA failed to request written feedback from FERC regarding potential reliability issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC's Office of Electric Reliability has expertise and statutory responsibility to 'coordinate with the applicable federal agencies ... to facilitate energy reliability and security.' EPA should engage FERC in an open, transparent process to assess reliability risks and solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume sufficient natural gas generation, pipeline capacity, or storage availability
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot assume the availability of sufficient natural gas generation or transportation/storage capacity to support environmental dispatch; events like the Polar Vortex demonstrated that heavy reliance on gas-fired generation can push the system to its limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firm pipeline transportation may not be available or economically feasible during peak demand; even contracted firm service was sometimes curtailed. Examples include extreme price spikes and curtailed deliveries during the 2014 Polar Vortex and impacts on specific cooperative plants (e.g., Hoosier Energy's Holland Energy).

rubrics_metrics.name: State measures (e.g., CO2 taxes) aimed at changing dispatch may raise Commerce Clause or preemption challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: A State imposing a CO2 tax or other measure on in-state generation with the intent of affecting wholesale prices and dispatch in an interstate FERC market could face Commerce Clause challenges or be found to have interfered with FERC's exclusive jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example litigation: actions restricting electricity imports or imposing in-state preferences have been enjoined; North Dakota v. Swanson and other cases demonstrate legal risk. Even if a Commerce Clause challenge fails, courts may find preemption under FERC authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gas-electric coordination and scheduling constraints impose real operational risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in operational structures between natural gas and electricity markets, and constraints on pipeline scheduling and deliveries during extreme events, can prevent gas-fired generators from procuring fuel to meet electricity market commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC investigations and orders (e.g., FERC Scheduling Coordination Order) and NERC assessments highlight the crucial interconnection between gas pipelines and electric transmission operators; increased gas-electric dependency increases blackout risk under stress events.
